rv.q: By the time it reaches its happily-ever-after ending – the musical doesn’t pretend for a moment it won’t get there
But if bubblegum melodies, outfits that slay, and pectoral-forward fun is what you’re after, the shoe fits.

To dismiss the show as bad is perhaps hyperbolic, but this whimsical revision of the fairy tale is mostly uninspired and toothless in its attempts at contemporary relevance.
Instead, it’s surprisingly vulgar, sexed-up and dumbed-down: a parade of hustling women in bustiers and shirtless pec-rippling hunks.
Ultimately, “Bad Cinderella” proves there is something worse than a new musical being bad: being unoriginal.
The musical collapses at the center, because Cinderella is an attitudinal bore.

“Bad Cinderella,” directed here by Laurence Connor (“School of Rock”), even manages to gleefully reinforce the chronic social fixations — on beauty, vanity and wealth — that it purports to deem toxic.
"Bad Cinderella," which opened at the Imperial Theater Thursday night, isn't good.
It attempts to say barely anything, and it succeeds.
But, along with JoAnn M. Hunter’s choreography, in a few places, that’s about all this pretty terrible show has on its list of positives.
“Bad Cinderella” is the cheesiest and crudest of the lot.
But Bad Cinderella would have been better off staying home than going to the ball.
For this 75-year-old musical theater veteran’s latest creative journey, it’s as happy an ending as anyone could have expected.
Zippel also makes the executive decision to rhyme "Cinderella" with "Salmonella" which I will personally never forgive nor forget.
There’s a whiplash in tone, from sarcastic to sincere, that the the production simply can handle.
If not necessarily bad, “Bad Cinderella” (which often feels like “Cinderella” combined with “Shrek” and “Clueless”) isn’t exactly great either.
It’s a wonder this prince doesn’t follow his big brother’s lead and end up with a nice, simple, compliant chorus boy.
Whatever his motives, “Bad Cinderella” is Lloyd Webber’s least original musical.
Bad Cinderella lacks cohesion and succeeds only in pandering.
Sadly, your money can be spent better elsewhere than on this unnecessary (and, for the record, not all-that-child-friendly) take on the classic fairy tale.
Bad Cinderella is a strangely rudderless enterprise.
Overall, Bad Cinderella is way out of balance.
Though entertaining, it is neither a convincing satire nor a lush romance.
The sheer cynicism of the entire enterprise, designed to capitalize on the public’s seemingly insatiable appetite for irreverent fairy tale adaptations, is enough to turn a carriage into a pumpkin.

All through Andrew Lloyd Webber’s inane mish-mash of a Broadway musical Bad Cinderella (Imperial Theatre, booking to Sept 23) the nagging question is: what makes this Cinderella “bad” in any interesting, intriguing, meaningfully different way? The answer: not much.
“Bad Cinderella” is entertaining and fast-paced
Bad Cinderella has budget and scale but lives up to its name in almost all elements.
Bad Cinderella is a trite, inflated children’s show, with a wit and intelligence quotient that does little to enhance Broadway’s IQ.

cn.t: Critics savage Lloyd Webber's fairy tale update as confused, tasteless, and rudderless, with most finding it inept despite occasional entertainment. Carolee Carmello's stepmother performance stands out in an otherwise chaotic misfire.

sg.ra: Imperial's auditorium is rectangular and wider than it is deep, so you lose very little distance moving back from the premium C-G band — and once you clear the mezzanine overhang (which hangs over Orchestra row H) the rake picks up enough to see over heads. Multiple Chess (2026) and Water for Elephants (2024) sitters in rows H-P described a dead-center full-stage view at sub-premium prices; one Chess viewer at Orch C H106 called it 'the best broadway seats I've had.' Seatplan, TickPick, and Headout independently pick this same band as the value tier.

TickPick and Seatplan both explicitly recommend Front Mezz row C and back (centered) over rows A-B, because the Imperial's front-mezz railing sits high enough to clip the stage for front-row sitters — a Water for Elephants viewer at Front Mezz R A401 (self-reported 6'3") wrote 'The bar definitely gets in the way… Avoid.' Rows C-F clear that bar while keeping the whole-stage overhead view that's the main reason to choose mezzanine over orchestra at Imperial.

sg.vl: Steep rake saves the cheap seats
sg.ra: Imperial has no elevators/escalators and the rear mezz is a real climb (one Chess sitter called it 'quite the hike'), but the rake is steep enough that several Chess and Smash viewers reported unobstructed full-stage views from rows A-C even with tall people in front ('Rake is good so most likely no heads blocking the stage,' 'Theater has a good rake so you can see over the person in front of you'). TickPick and Headout both specifically recommend rear-mezz center (not sides) as the cheap-seat sweet spot here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang, far from the action
sg.ra: Imperial is wider than it is deep, so the penalty for sitting far back is real — you lose closeness without gaining much sightline, and the same mid-tier price bracket gets you a few rows forward.
